title: Two recorders
hookLine: two angels record, not a word is uttered without a watcher ready (50:17–18)

lines: A TURN TO THE RIGHT, THEN THE LEFT.
THE TWO VERSES AFTER THE JUGULAR.
cards: At the end of the prayer, a Muslim turns the head to the right, then to the left, saying peace be upon you each time. Children who watch sometimes ask who is being greeted, since nobody seems to be there.
It's a fair question. Some teachers answer: the angels on either side, among others. That answer leans, in part, on Surah Qaf, in the two verses right after the jugular.

teach.h: ONE ON THE RIGHT, ONE ON THE LEFT.
teach.b: Verses seventeen and eighteen, in Pickthall's translation: "When the two Receivers receive (him), seated on the right hand and on the left, He uttereth no word but there is with him an observer ready."
Two receivers, the mutalaqqiyan, one on the right and one on the left. In Surah Al-Infitar, the Qur'an calls them kiraman katibin, noble writers. Popular teaching names them Raqib and 'Atid.
But raqib and 'atid are the words in verse eighteen meaning watcher and ready, and some commentators read them as descriptions, one watcher who is ready, rather than names.
The striking line is the second: not a word. Every sentence, the kind ones, the sharp ones, the ones you were sure nobody heard. That could sound frightening, and the verse means it seriously.
But the hadith tradition tilts the scale in an unexpected direction. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ says that when someone intends a good deed and doesn't do it, it's written as one good deed.
If they do it, ten or more. When someone intends a bad deed and holds back, it's written as a good deed. If they do it, it's written as one.
So the record is not neutral.
It's generous; mercy is built into the ledger. What the verse asks for is not paralysis. It's weight: the sense that words count.

how: Muslims close each prayer by turning right and left with the greeting of peace, and some teachers explain it as greeting, among others, the recording angels; guarding the tongue is a constant theme of Muslim ethical teaching.

o: two witnesses required to sign a contract
two angels writing down every word and deed
two prophets who wrote down the scriptures

s: the verse names the angels Raqib and 'Atid
some commentators read those words as descriptions, watcher and ready; the names are popular.
an intended good deed not done is still written as a good deed
a bad deed held back is written against you
the hadith says it's written as a good deed.

games.q: you intend a bad deed, then hold back. according to the hadith in Bukhari, what's written?
games.why: holding back is written as a good deed: mercy built into the ledger.

practice: Turn your head gently to the right and rest, then to the left and rest. Think back over what you've said so far today: which words would you like written, and which would you take back?
Don't judge; just notice, and if you pray, you can ask forgiveness for a careless word.

wordCard.voice: Two recorders. The receivers on the right and left in 50:17 and 18, before whom no word is spoken without a watcher ready. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: every word written. And the ledger leans toward mercy. That's day five hundred ninety.

sources.q: When the two Receivers receive (him), seated on the right hand and on the left, He uttereth no word but there is with him an observer ready.
